modules.title: Meaning and Scope of Commerce
modules.html:
What is Commerce?

Commerce is the aggregate of all activities concerned with the distribution and exchange of goods and services from producers to final consumers, together with the aids that make such exchange possible. It removes the barriers of place, time, knowledge, finance and risk that stand between production and consumption.

Scope of Commerce

  1. Trade – the actual buying and selling of goods; sub-divided into home trade (retail and wholesale) and foreign trade (import, export and entrepot).
  2. Aids to trade (ancillaries) – transportation, warehousing, banking, insurance, advertising, communication and tourism.

Commerce, Trade and Industry

TermMeaningExample
IndustryExtraction, processing and construction – creation of form utilityCement manufacture
TradeBuying and selling onlyA supermarket
CommerceTrade + all aids to tradeTrade, banking, insurance, haulage

Importance of Commerce

  • Bridges the gap between producers and consumers.
  • Creates employment and raises the standard of living.
  • Encourages large-scale production and specialisation.
  • Generates government revenue through duties and taxes.
  • Promotes international understanding and the transfer of technology.

Barriers to Trade and Their Removers

BarrierRemover
Place (distance)Transportation
Time (seasonality)Warehousing
FinanceBanking
RiskInsurance
IgnoranceAdvertising & communication
ExchangeMoney and trade

examples.q: A farmer in Benue harvests yams that are sold in Lagos six months later. Identify the commercial services that made this possible and the utility each created.
examples.a: Transportation moved the yams from Benue to Lagos, creating place utility. Warehousing stored them for six months, creating time utility. Banking financed the purchase and payment, insurance carried the risk of spoilage/theft, while advertising informed Lagos buyers (knowledge). The trader who finally sold them created possession utility.

examples.q: Distinguish between commerce and industry using a bakery as illustration.
examples.a: Industry is the baking of flour, sugar and yeast into bread – form utility. Commerce covers the purchase of flour, haulage of bread to shops, storage, the insurance of the delivery van, the bank overdraft financing raw materials and the radio advert. Industry produces; commerce distributes and supports.

modules.title: Occupation and Its Divisions
modules.html:
Meaning

An occupation is the economic activity a person engages in regularly to earn a living. Occupations are broadly divided into three.

1. Industrial Occupation

  • Extractive – taking materials from nature: farming, fishing, mining, lumbering, quarrying.
  • Manufacturing – converting raw materials into finished goods: textiles, cement, food processing.
  • Constructive – assembling finished materials into structures: roads, bridges, buildings, ships.

2. Commercial Occupation

Trade and aids to trade: retailers, wholesalers, bankers, insurers, shipping agents, advertisers, warehouse keepers.

3. Service (Direct/Personal) Occupation

  • Direct services – rendered to individuals: doctors, teachers, lawyers, barbers, musicians.
  • Indirect services – rendered to the community: police, soldiers, civil servants, firefighters.

Factors Determining Choice of Occupation

  1. Level of education, skill and aptitude
  2. Remuneration and fringe benefits
  3. Availability of capital
  4. Prestige and job security
  5. Family background, environment and government policy

examples.q: Classify the following: (i) a Warri crude oil driller (ii) a Kano wholesaler of textiles (iii) an Ibadan nurse (iv) a Julius Berger bridge builder.
examples.a: (i) Industrial – extractive. (ii) Commercial – trade. (iii) Service – direct service. (iv) Industrial – constructive.

examples.q: Why are commercial and service occupations described as 'non-productive' by some writers, and why is this wrong?
examples.a: They create no tangible goods, so critics call them unproductive. But production is complete only when goods reach the consumer; a doctor, banker or retailer creates utility and satisfies wants, so both are genuinely productive.

modules.title: Production, Factors of Production and Utility
modules.html:
Meaning of Production

Production is the creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants. It is complete only when the goods reach the final consumer.

Types of Production

  1. Primary – extractive activities.
  2. Secondary – manufacturing and construction.
  3. Tertiary – commercial and service activities.

Factors of Production and Their Rewards

FactorMeaningReward
LandAll free gifts of natureRent
LabourHuman physical and mental effortWages/Salaries
CapitalMan-made assets used to produce further wealthInterest
EntrepreneurOrganiser and risk-bearerProfit

Division of Labour and Specialisation

Splitting production into separate tasks performed by different people. Advantages: greater output, higher skill, saving of time, use of machinery, lower unit cost. Disadvantages: monotony, over-dependence, risk of unemployment, loss of craftsmanship.

Utility

Utility is the ability of a good or service to satisfy a want. Forms: form utility (manufacturing), place utility (transport), time utility (storage), possession utility (trade).

Basic Business Measures

Two measures used throughout the course:

$$\text{Working Capital} = \text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Employed} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$

Profit as a percentage of turnover is \( \dfrac{\text{Net Profit}}{\text{Turnover}} \times 100 \).

examples.q: A trader has current assets of ₦850,000 and current liabilities of ₦320,000. Total assets are ₦1,500,000. Find the working capital and capital employed.
examples.a: Working Capital \( = 850{,}000 - 320{,}000 = ₦530{,}000 \). Capital Employed \( = 1{,}500{,}000 - 320{,}000 = ₦1{,}180{,}000 \). The positive working capital shows the business can settle short-term debts and still finance daily operations.

examples.q: A tailoring workshop of 5 workers sews 40 shirts a day. After introducing division of labour output rises to 75 shirts. Calculate the percentage increase and state two dangers of the change.
examples.a: Increase \( = \dfrac{75-40}{40} \times 100 = 87.5\% \). Dangers: monotony leading to low morale, and over-dependence – the absence of one specialist can halt the whole line.

quiz.q: Commerce may best be defined as
options: Trade and all aids to trade
quiz.solution: Commerce = trade (buying and selling) PLUS the ancillaries such as banking, insurance, transport, warehousing, advertising and communication.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an aid to trade?
quiz.solution: Mining is an extractive (industrial) activity, not an aid to trade.

quiz.q: The barrier of distance in trade is removed by
quiz.solution: Transport moves goods from where they are produced to where they are needed, creating place utility.
Storing goods until they are needed creates time utility.

quiz.q: Fishing, mining and lumbering are examples of
quiz.solution: They take materials directly from nature.

quiz.q: The reward for the entrepreneur is
quiz.solution: The entrepreneur organises the other factors and bears risk; the residual reward is profit.
Services rendered to the community as a whole are indirect services.
Tertiary production covers commerce and services.
Working capital measures short-term liquidity: current assets less current liabilities.
Capital employed = total assets − current liabilities, i.e. long-term funds tied down in the business.

quiz.q: A major disadvantage of division of labour is
quiz.solution: Repeating one task all day makes work monotonous and reduces job satisfaction.

quiz.q: Which factor of production earns rent?
quiz.solution: Rent is the reward for land, the free gift of nature.

quiz.q: Converting cocoa beans into chocolate creates
quiz.solution: Changing the physical form of a good creates form utility.

quiz.q: Production is said to be complete when
options: Goods are stored in a warehouse
quiz.solution: Until the consumer's want is satisfied, production is incomplete.

quiz.q: Entrepot trade is a branch of
quiz.solution: Entrepot (re-export) trade is the importation of goods for onward export, a branch of foreign trade.

quiz.q: Which of these best determines a person's choice of occupation?
options: Number of workers in the town
quiz.solution: Aptitude/skill, available capital, pay and security are the recognised determinants.
